article.title: Why More Information Can Sometimes Make a Decision Worse
article.why: Learn when additional evidence improves a decision and when it only adds noise, bias, or delay.
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

sources.label: Background: decision analysis and value of information

paragraphs.en:
Modern decision makers rarely suffer from a complete absence of information. More often, they face an abundance of reports, dashboards, articles, forecasts, expert opinions, customer comments, and model outputs. Because information can reduce uncertainty, it is tempting to assume that collecting more of it must improve a decision. That assumption is not always true.

Information has value when it can change a decision in a way that improves expected outcomes. If a new analysis cannot plausibly alter the choice, or if it arrives after the decision must be made, its practical value may be close to zero. Worse, additional information can impose costs: time, attention, confusion, delay, and greater exposure to selective evidence.

Consider a team choosing between two product designs. After several user tests, the evidence strongly favors Design A. The team could run another twenty interviews. Those interviews might reveal something important, but they also delay launch by three weeks. The relevant question is not whether more information would be interesting. It is whether its expected decision value exceeds the cost of waiting.

Noise is one problem. When many weak signals are collected, decision makers may struggle to distinguish meaningful evidence from random variation. A dashboard with fifty metrics can make almost any story appear plausible. Some indicators will improve while others deteriorate simply by chance. Without a hierarchy of evidence, more data can increase narrative flexibility rather than knowledge.

Confirmation bias creates another risk. People do not process all evidence neutrally. When information is abundant, they can selectively focus on sources that support their preferred conclusion. Searching longer may therefore increase confidence without improving accuracy. The person is not necessarily learning; they may be accumulating arguments.

Redundancy also matters. Ten reports may appear to be ten independent pieces of evidence even when all of them rely on the same original dataset or assumption. Repetition can create an illusion of corroboration. Good decision processes trace sources and ask whether new evidence is genuinely independent.

Information overload can also weaken attention. Human working memory is limited, and complex choices require prioritization. When every detail is presented as important, decision makers may spend cognitive effort on low-value distinctions while overlooking the few variables that actually determine the outcome.

This is why stopping rules are useful. Before gathering more evidence, a team can specify what uncertainty remains, what new information would change the decision, how much time or money it is worth spending, and when analysis will stop. For example: “We will run two additional tests only if they can distinguish whether the defect rate is below our 1 percent launch threshold.” This links information collection to a decision boundary.

A related concept is value of information. In formal decision analysis, information is valuable because it can improve the action chosen under uncertainty. Perfect information would reveal the true state before acting, while imperfect information only changes probabilities. In practice, teams rarely need a full mathematical model to use the intuition. They can ask: What decision would we make now? What result from the next analysis would cause us to choose differently? How likely is that result? What is the benefit of changing course?

Timing matters as much as content. Waiting can be valuable when a decision is irreversible and new evidence is likely to arrive soon. But delay is costly when opportunities decay, competitors move, or implementation itself generates learning. The optimal amount of information therefore depends on reversibility, stakes, uncertainty, and time pressure.

Filtering is not the same as ignoring inconvenient evidence. A good filter is defined before seeing the answer. It prioritizes source quality, relevance to the decision, independence, and expected ability to change action. This protects against both indiscriminate data accumulation and motivated exclusion.

Organizations can improve decisions by separating exploratory information from decision-critical evidence. Exploration can remain broad, but the final decision memo should identify the few assumptions, metrics, and uncertainties that matter most. It should also state what evidence would falsify the preferred recommendation.

More information is therefore not automatically better. The objective is not to maximize the number of facts collected; it is to reduce decision-relevant uncertainty at a reasonable cost. Sometimes one additional experiment is worth months of debate. At other times, another report only postpones an uncomfortable choice.

A mature decision process knows both how to seek evidence and how to stop seeking it. Information filtering, explicit decision thresholds, source independence, and stopping rules help transform an abundance of data into disciplined judgment. The best question is not “Can we learn more?” but “Would learning more be likely to change what we should do?”
paragraphs.zh: 更多資訊不必然帶來更好的決策。資訊的價值在於它是否可能改變行動並改善預期結果；如果新分析不太可能改變選擇，或取得資訊造成的等待成本過高，繼續蒐集資料可能反而降低決策品質。大量弱訊號會增加 noise，資訊過多也可能讓人透過 confirmation bias 選擇性尋找支持既有立場的證據。重複引用同一資料來源還可能製造虛假的 corroboration。實務上可預先設定 stopping rule：還剩什麼不確定性、哪種結果會改變決策、最多願意花多少時間與成本。Value of information 的核心不是『還能不能知道更多』，而是『知道更多是否可能改變應採取的行動』。好的 filtering 應在看到答案前定義，依來源品質、相關性、獨立性與改變決策的能力篩選證據。
paragraphs.ja: 情報は多いほど良いとは限りません。追加情報に価値があるのは、それによって選択する行動が変わり、期待成果が改善する可能性があるときです。弱いシグナルを大量に集めるとnoiseが増え、confirmation biasによって自分の結論を支持する情報だけを選びやすくなります。同じ元データに依存する複数レポートを独立した証拠と誤認する危険もあります。実務では、何が分かれば意思決定を変えるのか、追加分析にどこまで時間・費用を使うのか、いつ分析を止めるのかを事前に決めるstopping ruleが有効です。重要なのは情報量の最大化ではなく、意思決定に関係する不確実性を合理的なコストで減らすことです。

vocabulary.usage: Decision makers often face an abundance of information.
Weak signals can add noise rather than knowledge.
Abundant information can amplify confirmation bias.
Check whether apparent evidence is actually redundant.
Repeated sources can create an illusion of corroboration.
Define a stopping rule before gathering more evidence.
Information value depends partly on decision reversibility.
State what evidence would falsify the recommendation.
Link additional analysis to a decision threshold.
Avoid selective use of supporting evidence.

phrases.explanation: 判斷資訊是否真正具有 decision value 的核心問法。
phrases.example: Would the next analysis change what we should do?

grammar.title: not whether A, but whether B
grammar.body: 把問題從次要判準轉向真正的決策判準，例如：The question is not whether more data are interesting, but whether they can change the decision.

business.term: What result would actually change the decision?
business.explanation: 在追加分析前先定義 decision-changing evidence。
business.example: Before commissioning another study, what result would actually change the decision?
We have enough evidence for the current choice; what is our stopping rule for additional research?

quiz.question: When does additional information have high practical value?
quiz.answer: When it has a meaningful chance of changing the chosen action in a way that improves expected outcomes, after considering the cost of obtaining it.
